qs.q: An unvaccinated child develops sudden fever, conjunctivitis, and pharyngitis after swimming in a public pool. The school nurse notes several other students have similar symptoms. Which diagnostic feature characterizes the causative agent?
o: Non-enveloped single-stranded DNA virus causing severe pure red cell aplasia.
Enveloped single-stranded RNA virus with segmented genome and spikes.
Non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus with characteristic capsid fiber projections.
Enveloped double-stranded DNA virus establishing life-long sensory latency.
Non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus showing resistance to acid environments.
qs.e: Adenoviruses are non-enveloped dsDNA viruses with fiber proteins at the capsid vertices that cause pharyngoconjunctival fever.

qs.q: A public health laboratory investigates an outbreak of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis characterized by severe ocular pain and subconjunctival hemorrhages. Which viral family is most frequently implicated in causing these explosive epidemics?
o: Adenoviridae pathogens producing robust cytopathic effects in corneal epithelium
Picornaviridae members utilizing specific intercellular adhesion molecule receptors
Paramyxoviridae agents entering through respiratory droplets and eye contact
Herpesviridae entities establishing lifelong latency in trigeminal ganglia
Poxviridae species causing localized umbilicated nodules on eyelid margins
qs.e: Enteroviruses within Picornaviridae, particularly Enterovirus D70 and Coxsackie A24, cause acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.

qs.q: Outbreaks of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis in tropical regions are mainly caused by which viral group?
qs.e: Enteroviruses of the Picornaviridae family, especially coxsackie A24, cause hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.

qs.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a 6-day history of high fever, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy greater than 1.5 cm, red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, and bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis. What is the primary therapeutic goal of urgent intervention?
qs.e: These findings are diagnostic of Kawasaki disease, which requires urgent intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin to prevent coronary artery aneurysms. Renal scarring is a complication associated with urinary tract infections rather than this vasculitis.

qs.q: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis outbreaks are primarily caused by which of the following viral groups?
qs.e: Enterovirus 70 and Coxsackievirus A24 are the primary causative agents of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis. Other respiratory or enteric groups do not typically present with this specific syndrome.

qs.q: A patient presents with keratitis, conjunctivitis, and iritis following a shingles outbreak. Which nerve involvement is likely responsible for these symptoms?
o: Involvement of the thoracic dorsal root ganglion
qs.e: Trigeminal nerve involvement in zoster can lead to ocular complications like keratitis, conjunctivitis, and iritis. Sacral nerves are involved in genital herpes, and facial nerve involvement causes Bell's palsy.

qs.q: A young adult presents with sudden severe eye pain, swelling, and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Which viral family does the causative agent of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis belong to?
qs.e: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is caused by enteroviruses, which are members of the Picornaviridae family. Paramyxoviridae includes viruses such as mumps and measles.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and conjunctivitis. The symptoms are similar to streptococcal pharyngitis. Which virus is most likely responsible for this presentation?
qs.e: Adenoviruses, particularly serotypes 1-7, are common in pediatric populations and can cause acute febrile pharyngitis that mimics strep throat in children under 3 years old. Serotypes 4 & 7 are associated with Acute Respiratory Disease (ARD), and serotypes 40-42 with gastroenteritis.

ai.title: Conjunctivitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, usually infectious or allergic. Rapid bedside assessment and simple tests guide treatment, especially in low‑resource settings where advanced labs may be unavailable.

sections.p: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctival mucosa. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by simple tests when available.
b: Redness, tearing, discharge, itching or pain
History of contact, travel, or recent illness

t.b: Detects corneal ulceration – a white spot on the cornea indicates ulcer
Distinguishes bacterial (Gram‑positive cocci or Gram‑negative rods) from viral or allergic causes; a positive Gram stain suggests bacterial conjunctivitis

sections.p: Severity is graded by the extent of ocular involvement and systemic signs.
b: Moderate: bilateral, purulent discharge, mild pain
Severe: bilateral pain, corneal involvement, vision loss

t.b: Assesses corneal involvement – loss of vision suggests keratitis

sections.p: Etiology is grouped by infectious, allergic, irritant, and systemic causes.
b: Bacterial (Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae)

t.b: Positive indicates viral conjunctivitis; negative does not exclude other viral causes

sections.p: History and examination reveal characteristic patterns.
b: Bacterial: purulent discharge, eyelid edema, pain, possible eyelash involvement
Viral: watery discharge, follicular conjunctivitis, preceding URI
Allergic: itching, bilateral, associated with seasonal allergens, pale conjunctiva

t.b: High osmolarity suggests dry eye or allergic conjunctivitis

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, investigations are limited but targeted.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a child with purulent eye discharge?
faq.a: Apply a topical antibiotic drop (e.g., ciprofloxacin) and advise hand hygiene.

faq.q: When is a corneal scrape indicated?
faq.a: When there is corneal ulceration or loss of vision.

faq.q: Can allergic conjunctivitis be treated with steroids?
faq.a: Only if severe and after antihistamines; avoid in viral or bacterial cases.

exam: A 5‑year‑old presents with red, watery eyes and a preceding cough. What is the most likely cause? — Adenoviral conjunctivitis; look for follicular conjunctiva and consider measles if rash appears.

A patient with purulent discharge and eyelid edema is started on erythromycin ointment. What is the next step if symptoms persist after 48 hours? — Re‑evaluate for bacterial resistance; consider switching to fluoroquinolone drops.
A 30‑year‑old with HIV presents with eye pain and vision loss. What complication should you suspect? — HIV‑associated keratoconjunctivitis or opportunistic infection like CMV retinitis.
You suspect trachoma in a rural child. What clinical sign confirms it? — Follicular conjunctivitis with scarring and trichiasis.
A patient reports itching and bilateral redness after a pollen season. What first‑line therapy is appropriate? — Antihistamine eye drops and mast cell stabilisers.
A child has red eye and a fever of 38.5°C. Which test should you perform first? — Rapid viral antigen test for adenovirus; if negative, consider bacterial culture.
A patient with conjunctivitis refuses to use eye drops. What non‑pharmacologic advice can you give? — Warm compresses, frequent hand washing, and avoiding contact lenses.
